lens: D — the conformance engine and the decoders (ts/src/evaluate/**, ts/src/decode/**): are behaviour-changing mutations killed by the suite, or is only the happy path pinned?

findings.title: EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW's lower bound is pinned by nothing in either gate profile: a future-dated mandate ALLOWs and every comparison surface stays identical
findings.surface: ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts:288-293 (EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW); ts/test/evaluate.checks.test.ts:227; ts/src/corpus/fixtures.ts:288-295 (F033); scripts/test.sh corpus stage
findings.claim: Deleting the `now >= mandate.validAfter &&` half of EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW leaves the entire TypeScript suite green (405/405) AND leaves both artifacts the deep-profile corpus stage compares byte-identical to a clean run — while F033, the corpus fixture written for exactly this condition ('A mandate whose validAfter is in the future'), flips L2 and L3 from BLOCK/['EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW'] to ALLOW/[]. The only test case for this code perturbs `validUntil` only, so the upper bound is tested and the lower bound is not. The one artifact in the repository that would move is `fixtures/corpus/results/F033.json`, which no gate profile regenerates and compares (`grep -c results scripts/test.sh` → 0).
findings.why_it_matters: A mandate the owner signed but that has not yet come into force is accepted as authorisation. The engine's verdict and the evidence bundle both say ALLOW. The deployed pipeline does not execute it — ts/src/signer/attest.ts:397 re-checks the same window and pushes SIGNER_MANDATE_WINDOW (CONFORMANCE tier, which refuses ALLOW) — so this is a pinning defect rather than a live exploit. But the project's stated bar for whether the verdicts are right is the corpus, the corpus HAS the fixture, and the fixture's result is compared against nothing; the check is therefore free to rot in any future edit and nothing anywhere would go red.
findings.reproduction:
cd <worktree>; python3 replace in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts: 'now >= mandate.validAfter && now <= mandate.validUntil,' -> 'now <= mandate.validUntil,' (2 changed lines, verified by diff).
(1) cd ts && npm --prefix ts test  ->  'ℹ tests 405 / ℹ pass 405 / ℹ fail 0'  (control on the unmutated tree: identical 405/405).
(2) Direct behaviour probe (a small driver importing ts/src/evaluate/index.ts, built in ts/ so node_modules resolves): unmutated -> 'D1 mandate validAfter in the FUTURE  verdict=BLOCK reasonCodes=["EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW"]'; mutated -> 'verdict=ALLOW reasonCodes=[]'. Five other rows in the same probe (baseline ALLOW, policy window, action binding, ceiling boundary, deadline boundary) are unchanged, so the probe is targeted, not blanket.
(3) Corpus arm. `ts/src/corpus/run.ts:194` builds a unix socket under the repo root; in this worktree that path exceeds macOS's 104-byte sun_path limit and the run aborts with EINVAL, so I temporarily repointed it to /tmp/sD/${port}.sock (and restored it afterwards). With that, two corpus runs into separate temp dirs, clean vs mutated: `_digests.json` digests block IDENTICAL (True); all 50 committed-view files IDENTICAL under the deep gate's own normalisation function (differing: 0); results/ layer verdicts differ on exactly one fixture — F033.json, L2 and L3 both ('BLOCK',('EVAL_MANDATE_WINDOW',)) -> ('ALLOW',()); results/_index.json differs. On the unmutated tree the same results comparison against the committed files reports 'fixtures whose layer verdict/failing set MOVED: 0', which is the control proving the comparator is live.
findings.probe_moved_something: The direct probe moved one verdict from BLOCK to ALLOW and emptied its reasonCodes, leaving five sibling rows untouched. The corpus probe moved exactly one fixture's L2/L3 verdicts and made results/_index.json differ, while leaving the digest block and all 50 normalised view files bit-identical. Two controls bracket the harness: a comment-only edit to the same file SURVIVED (243/243), and deleting the EVAL_PURCHASE_BENEFICIARY check was KILLED by the named test.

findings.title: EVAL_POLICY_WINDOW's lower bound has zero coverage anywhere in the repository — no test, no corpus fixture, no sample
findings.claim: Deleting `now >= policy.validAfter &&` leaves the full TypeScript suite green (405/405). Unlike D-01 this one has no witness at all: the single test case perturbs `validUntil`; the corpus has F032 for the policy's UPPER bound (`env: {advancePastPolicyWindow: true}`) and nothing for its lower bound; every `validAfter` in ts/test/**, fixtures/samples/** and ts/src/corpus/fixtures.ts is `0` except F033's MANDATE validAfter. So even regenerating and comparing the corpus results — the fix D-01 implies — would not catch this one.
findings.why_it_matters: A policy that has been signed and activated but has not yet come into force is treated as in force. Same second line of defence as D-01 (ts/src/signer/attest.ts:421 pushes SIGNER_POLICY_WINDOW), so again a pinning defect rather than a live bypass — but it is strictly worse-covered than D-01, and the two sit two lines apart in the same `results.push(...)` call, which is exactly the 'repair generalised the demonstration, not the argument' shape this project has shipped before.
findings.reproduction:
Replace in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts: 'now >= policy.validAfter && now <= policy.validUntil,' -> 'now <= policy.validUntil,'.
(1) npm --prefix ts test -> 'ℹ pass 405 / ℹ fail 0'.
(2) Direct probe: unmutated 'D2 policy validAfter in the FUTURE verdict=BLOCK reasonCodes=["EVAL_POLICY_WINDOW"]' -> mutated 'verdict=ALLOW reasonCodes=[]', with the mandate-window row still BLOCK (so the two mutations are independent and each probe is targeted).
(3) Coverage claim verified by: grep -rn 'validAfter' ts/test ts/src fixtures/samples | grep -v 'validAfter: 0n' — the only non-zero occurrences are differential.test.ts's random hash generator (hashing only, never the evaluator) and corpus F033's MANDATE.
findings.probe_moved_something: One verdict moved BLOCK->ALLOW; the sibling mandate-window row did not move. Same two harness controls as D-01.

findings.title: No gate profile compares the corpus's engine verdicts — and the deep stage's two comparison arms are provably blind to a verdict flip. The register's recorded bound for this gap is understated.
findings.surface: scripts/test.sh (§7.1 corpus stage, the `_digests.json` diff and the VIEWCHECK heredoc); fixtures/corpus/results/*.json and _index.json; ts/src/corpus/leakage.ts (FORBIDDEN_KEYS); docs/v1-1-register.md §8.4
findings.claim: `docs/v1-1-register.md` §8.4 records that `fixtures/corpus/results/*.json` is 'a committed artifact that nothing regenerates-and-compares', and frames the consequence as a laundering route into `check-class-coverage.sh` — i.e. someone EDITS A COMMITTED JSON FILE. The bound is larger than that. The same gap means the engine's verdicts on all 50 fixtures are pinned by nothing, so an edit to ts/src/evaluate/**, not to any artifact, is equally invisible. I measured both deep-stage arms against a real verdict flip: the `_digests.json` digests block is IDENTICAL between a clean corpus run and one under the D-01 mutation, and all 50 view files are IDENTICAL under the stage's own normalisation. That is not an accident of this mutation — the labeller views are verdict-free BY CONSTRUCTION: `assertNoLeakage` forbids `verdict`, `engineVerdict`, `l3Verdict`, `computedLabel`, `expectedOutcome`, `failingChecks`, `evaluatorReasonCodes`, `layerVerdicts`. So the deep gate re-executes the corpus and then compares the one output stream that is designed to carry no verdict.
findings.why_it_matters: HANDOFF and both evaluate/ module headers say the engine's bar is 'the independently labelled corpus, never its own suite'. The corpus is executed at the gate; its verdicts are compared to nothing. That is the difference between 'the corpus is the bar' and 'the corpus is run'. It is also the mechanical explanation for the 21 survivors in this round: the surface that would notice a verdict change is not compared by any profile.
findings.reproduction:
(1) `grep -c results scripts/test.sh` -> 0 (reproduces the register's own measurement).
(2) Read scripts/test.sh's corpus stage: it diffs `$CORPUS_TMP/for-labelling/_digests.json` against the committed one, then runs a python VIEWCHECK over `for-labelling/` only. `$CORPUS_TMP/results/` is written and deleted unread.
(3) Two corpus runs (clean, and under the D-01 mutation) into separate SENTINEL_CORPUS_OUT dirs, compared to each other: digests block identical -> True; view files compared 50, differing under the gate's normalisation -> 0; 32 of 50 view files differ byte-for-byte but only in the expiry fields the stage normalises; results fixtures whose verdict/failing MOVED -> 1 (F033: L2 and L3 BLOCK->ALLOW); results/_index.json identical -> False.
(4) Control: the same results comparison, clean run vs COMMITTED files, reports 0 moved — so a results/ comparison would be a working check if it existed.
findings.probe_moved_something: The clean-vs-mutated corpus pair moved results/_index.json and one results file while leaving both gate comparison artifacts bit-identical. The clean-vs-committed control moved nothing, proving the comparator is not simply reporting noise.

findings.title: reasonCodes can be emptied of every UNRESOLVED code and the whole 405-test suite stays green — Case 4 then issues a REVIEW receipt that states no reason
findings.surface: ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts:521-524 (failingCodes); consumed as EvaluationResult.reasonCodes and hashed into the receipt's reasonCodesHash
findings.claim: Changing `failingCodes`'s predicate from `r.outcome !== "PASS"` to `r.outcome === "VIOLATION"` — dropping every UNRESOLVED code from the receipt — survives the full TypeScript suite (405/405), including ts/test/cases.e2e.test.ts and ts/test/reasoncodes.test.ts. On the §4.2 Case 4 input (target code-hash mismatch, failureMode = REVIEW) the engine then returns verdict=REVIEW with reasonCodes=[] where the unmutated engine returns ["EVAL_TARGET_CODE_IDENTITY"].
findings.why_it_matters: The reason codes are the only thing on a REVIEW receipt that says why it is a review, and reasonCodesHash is what the receipt commits to. A REVIEW with an empty reason list is a receipt that says 'a human must look at this' and does not say at what — and Case 4 is a ratified demonstration case whose e2e test passes with the list empty. The evidence bundle's `unresolvedChecks` still carries the code, so the information is not lost from the bundle; it is lost from the receipt.
findings.reproduction:
Replace in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts: 'return [...new Set(results.filter((r) => r.outcome !== "PASS").map((r) => r.code))].sort();' -> '... r.outcome === "VIOLATION" ...'.
npm --prefix ts test -> 'ℹ tests 405 / ℹ pass 405 / ℹ fail 0'.
Direct probe, code-hash-mismatch row: unmutated 'D6 code-hash mismatch (REVIEW)  verdict=REVIEW reasonCodes=["EVAL_TARGET_CODE_IDENTITY"]'; mutated 'verdict=REVIEW reasonCodes=[]'. The five BLOCK/ALLOW rows in the same probe are unchanged.
findings.probe_moved_something: One row's reasonCodes went from a one-element list to empty while its verdict and every other row held. Suite count stayed at exactly 405 pass / 0 fail, i.e. no test even changed shape.

findings.title: EVAL_ACTION_BINDS_MANDATE_AND_POLICY folds two conditions under one code and only the mandate half is exercised; the policy half can be deleted undetected
findings.claim: The check is `action.mandateHash === mandateHash && action.policyHash === policyHash`. Its only test case perturbs `action.mandateHash`. Dropping `&& action.policyHash === policyHash` survives 362 of the 405 tests (the anvil-free 243 plus cases.e2e, rulings, reasoncodes, decode.chain, differential and hardening); an action naming a policyHash unrelated to the presented and active policy then evaluates to ALLOW. §5.7.1 documents this code as 'the action names the hashes the vault reports active' — plural — so the deleted half is documented behaviour. The mirror mutation (dropping the mandate half) IS killed, which is what shows the asymmetry is in the test and not in the code.
findings.why_it_matters: §3.3(4)/(5)'s binding requirements rest on this code. A single code covering two independent bindings means the exhaustiveness guard in evaluate.checks.test.ts — which asserts every declared code FIRES — scores it covered while half its predicate has no witness. The vault re-checks action.policyHash on chain, so this is a pinning gap, not a live bypass.
findings.reproduction:
Replace in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts: 'action.mandateHash === mandateHash && action.policyHash === policyHash,' -> 'action.mandateHash === mandateHash,'.
cd ts && node --test --test-concurrency=1 test/evaluate.checks.test.ts test/decode.test.ts test/jcs.test.ts test/ablation.test.ts test/corpus.test.ts test/eip712.test.ts test/propose.test.ts test/canary.test.ts test/cases.e2e.test.ts test/rulings.test.ts test/reasoncodes.test.ts test/decode.chain.test.ts test/differential.test.ts test/hardening.test.ts -> 'ℹ pass 362 / ℹ fail 0' (control on the unmutated tree: identical 362/362).
Direct probe: unmutated 'D3 action.policyHash unbound from policy  verdict=BLOCK reasonCodes=["EVAL_ACTION_BINDS_MANDATE_AND_POLICY"]'; mutated 'verdict=ALLOW reasonCodes=[]'.
Mirror control: the same anchor -> 'action.policyHash === policyHash,' is KILLED by 'EVAL_ACTION_BINDS_MANDATE_AND_POLICY → VIOLATION' at 242/243.
findings.probe_moved_something: One verdict moved BLOCK->ALLOW. The mirror mutation moved the test count to 242 pass / 1 fail with the expected test named, proving the anchor region is live and the asymmetry is real. NOT confirmed against the full 405 — signer.e2e.test.ts, propose.e2e.test.ts, simulate.test.ts, attestor.concurrency.test.ts and keystore.test.ts were not run for this one (see coverage statement).

findings.title: Every ceiling and deadline comparison boundary in the engine is unpinned: <= can become < on all five and nothing fails
findings.claim: Each of these five tests perturbs the input STRICTLY past the limit (value = ceiling-1 as the ceiling, deadline = NOW-1), so `<=` and `<` are indistinguishable to the suite, and the ALLOW baseline sits far from every boundary (value 1000 against a 1e18 ceiling). All five `<= -> <` mutations survive the 362-test oracle. An action whose value is EXACTLY the mandate ceiling, or whose evaluation happens EXACTLY at its deadline second, then BLOCKs where the specification says it conforms.
findings.why_it_matters: The direction is fail-safe, so this is not a bypass — but 'value exactly at the ceiling' and 'now exactly at the deadline' are the two inputs an operator will actually hit, and D-006 sample-checking would show them as blocks with no bug anywhere the suite can see. More to the point for this lens: five checks that the exhaustiveness guard scores as covered have no boundary witness at all, which is the same 'the instrument names the check, not the predicate' shape recorded five times in this repository.
findings.reproduction:
Five independent edits in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts, each `<=` -> `<`: 'action.valueWei <= mandate.maxNativeValueWei,', 'action.valueWei <= policy.maxNativeValueWei,', 'action.valueWei <= vaultState.maxNativeValueWei,', 'require_(now <= action.deadline, "EVAL_ACTION_DEADLINE"', 'decoded.amount <= policy.maxAllowanceIncreaseBaseUnits,'.
Each: the 14-file 362-test run -> 'ℹ pass 362 / ℹ fail 0'. The mandate-ceiling one additionally survived the full 405-test suite is NOT claimed; only the 362 oracle was run for four of the five (the mandate-ceiling variant was measured at 362 only).
Direct probe, mandate-ceiling variant: unmutated 'D4 value exactly at the mandate ceiling  verdict=ALLOW reasonCodes=[]' -> mutated 'verdict=BLOCK reasonCodes=["EVAL_VALUE_WITHIN_MANDATE"]'. Deadline variant: unmutated 'D5 now == action.deadline exactly  verdict=ALLOW' -> mutated 'verdict=BLOCK reasonCodes=["EVAL_ACTION_DEADLINE"]'.
findings.probe_moved_something: Each variant moved exactly one probe row from ALLOW to BLOCK and left the other five rows identical — so each of the five boundaries was independently demonstrated to be reachable and unasserted.

findings.title: EVAL_EXECUTABILITY_CODES — D-026's remedy classification — is guarded against growing wrong and not against shrinking; members can be deleted silently
findings.claim: The three assertions on this set are: every member is a declared EVAL_ code; the set is non-empty (`size > 0`); and it does not overlap MANDATE_CONFORMANCE_CODES. None pins MEMBERSHIP. Removing 'EVAL_ACTION_DEADLINE' — one of the exactly four codes D-026's ruling names — survives the 362-test oracle. Three of the four could be removed and `size > 0` would still hold.
findings.why_it_matters: D-026 ruled that this set is what makes the REMEDY derivable by a reader holding the amended §3.3(7): unpause, use the current signer, propose less, re-propose before the deadline. A code that silently loses its classification is reported to that reader as a mandate violation requiring a new mandate, which is the exact wrong remedy D-026 was written to stop. It is also the shrink-blindness shape A-047 already found once (a verifier suite that could shrink undetected) and closed with floors in one place only.
findings.reproduction:
Delete the line '    "EVAL_ACTION_DEADLINE",' from the EVAL_EXECUTABILITY_CODES Set literal in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts (anchored on the preceding '"EVAL_VALUE_WITHIN_VAULT_CAP",' line so the edit is unique; diff shows 1 changed line).
cd ts && the 14-file 362-test run -> 'ℹ pass 362 / ℹ fail 0'. Also green on the anvil-free 243 subset.
Consumers verified by grep -rn EVAL_EXECUTABILITY_CODES ts/ scripts/ verifier/ docs/ — the only code reference outside its declaration is ts/test/ablation.test.ts:308-319.
findings.probe_moved_something: The diff removed one line from the array the guard reads (verified by diff, not assumed — this repository has shipped probes that injected code outside the array a guard reads). Test count stayed 362/362, i.e. the assertion that names this set ran and passed with a member missing.

findings.title: The decoder's strictness predicates are pinned by one witness each: an address word is only checked for dirt in its TOP byte, and a bool word of 3 can be accepted
findings.surface: ts/src/decode/abi.ts:119-140 (WordReader.address, WordReader.boolean); ts/test/decode.test.ts refusal table + 'the refusal table is exhaustive'
findings.claim: decode.test.ts has exactly one witness per DECODE_ failure code, and the exhaustiveness guard asserts each code FIRES — not that its predicate boundary is right. Both dirty-address witnesses put the dirt in byte 0 of the 12 high bytes ('ff'+11 zero bytes, '01'+11 zero bytes), so narrowing `w.slice(0, 24)` to `w.slice(0, 2)` survives — calldata with a non-zero byte anywhere in bytes 1..11 of an address word then decodes silently instead of raising DECODE_DIRTY_ADDRESS_BITS. The bool witness is the word `...02`, so widening `/^0*1$/` to `/^0*[13]$/` survives — a bool word of 3 decodes as `true` instead of DECODE_NON_CANONICAL_BOOL. Both survive the 362-test oracle including decode.chain.test.ts.
findings.why_it_matters: abi.ts's own header states the property these predicates exist for: 'every deviation from the exact encoding is a named failure rather than a shrug', and 'a decoder that accepts something it should not have produces a wrong allow'. The controls show the class is not uniformly unpinned — the trailing-bytes and uintN-width mutations ARE killed — so this is two specific holes, and it tells you what the refusal table measures: one point per code, not a boundary.
findings.reproduction:
Two independent edits in ts/src/decode/abi.ts.
(a) 'const high = w.slice(0, 24);' -> 'const high = w.slice(0, 2);'  -> 362-test run 'ℹ pass 362 / ℹ fail 0'.
(b) 'if (/^0*1$/.test(w)) return true;' -> 'if (/^0*[13]$/.test(w)) return true;'  -> 'ℹ pass 362 / ℹ fail 0'.
Controls in the same file that ARE killed, proving the probes are live and the file is under test: 'if (body.length !== expectedWords * WORD_HEX)' -> '<' is killed by 'refuses trailing bytes past the declared arguments with DECODE_LENGTH_MISMATCH' (242/243); 'const highNibbles = (256 - bits) / 4;' -> '... - 2;' is killed by 'refuses duration overflowing uint64 with DECODE_UINT_OVERFLOW' (242/243).
findings.probe_moved_something: The two sibling mutations in the same two functions moved the test count to 242/1 with the correctly-named tests failing, so the file is exercised and the two survivors are specific gaps rather than a dead probe.

findings.title: Three evidence-bundle fields are read by no assertion and can be made to state the opposite of what the engine computed
findings.claim: Three mutations to buildEvidenceBundle survive the 362-test oracle: hardcoding `targetCodeIdentity.matches: true` (so the bundle asserts code identity matched on the very input where EVAL_TARGET_CODE_IDENTITY is UNRESOLVED for the mismatch, two fields apart in the same object); filtering `unresolvedChecks` on `"VIOLATION"` instead of `"UNRESOLVED"` (so the field lists the wrong class); and turning `minOf` into a max (so `expectedEffects.maxNativeValueWei` publishes the LOOSER of the mandate and policy ceilings, inverting §5.2's 'constraints are intersected'). By contrast, filtering `policyChecks` down to failures only IS killed, by cases.e2e.test.ts:566 `assert.ok(policyChecks.some((c) => c.outcome === "PASS"))`.
findings.why_it_matters: §5.6's bundle is what a sceptical reader is handed at the five-minute comprehension gate and what D-010's verifier reproduces. These three fields would be read as facts and are asserted by nothing. The killed policyChecks mutation shows the bundle is not wholly untested — which makes the three survivors a list of specific fields worth one assertion each, not an argument for a rewrite.
findings.reproduction:
Three independent edits in ts/src/evaluate/index.ts, each followed by the 14-file 362-test run:
(a) 'matches: mandate.targetCodeHash.toLowerCase() === vaultState.targetCodeHash.toLowerCase(),' -> 'matches: true,'  -> 362/0.
(b) 'unresolvedChecks: checks.filter((c) => c.outcome === "UNRESOLVED").map((c) => c.code),' -> '... === "VIOLATION" ...'  -> 362/0.
(c) 'return a < b ? a : b;' inside minOf -> 'return a > b ? a : b;'  -> 362/0.
Control in the same function that IS killed: 'policyChecks: checks.map((c) => ({' -> 'policyChecks: checks.filter((c) => c.outcome !== "PASS").map((c) => ({'  -> 361 pass / 1 fail, 'carries all thirteen §5.6 fields and hashes deterministically' at test/cases.e2e.test.ts:531. (This control is also scripts/mutate.sh's own E11, so E11 is currently caught.)
findings.probe_moved_something: The control mutation in the same function moved the count to 361/1 and named the test, so buildEvidenceBundle is exercised; the three survivors are therefore specific unread fields.

findings.title: Address case-normalisation in the binding checks is unpinned in both directions
findings.claim: Removing `.toLowerCase()` from both sides of EVAL_TARGET_BOUND and of EVAL_SELECTOR_BOUND survives the 362-test oracle: every fixture in the suite spells its addresses and selectors in one case, so the normalisation is never exercised. Separately, changing EVAL_APPROVAL_SPENDER to compare the decoded spender against `mandate.principal` instead of `mandate.beneficiary` also survives — the fixtures set principal and beneficiary to the same address, so a mandate that authorises an approval to a beneficiary who is not the principal is checked against the wrong field with nothing noticing.
findings.why_it_matters: A-016/D-017 already produced one live case-normalisation defect (an uppercase-spelled beneficiary decoding differently and causing a spurious FATAL refusal), and ts/src/decode/abi.ts carries the rule 'two calldata strings differing only in hex spelling are the SAME BYTES'. The rule is enforced in the decoder and merely hoped for in the evaluator's own comparisons. The APPROVAL_SPENDER variant is the more interesting of the three because it is a wrong-field comparison rather than a normalisation, and the fixture makes the two fields equal.
findings.reproduction:
Three independent edits in ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts, each with the 14-file 362-test run:
(a) 'action.target.toLowerCase() === mandate.target.toLowerCase(),' -> 'action.target === mandate.target,' -> 362/0.
(b) 'decode.selector.toLowerCase() === mandate.selector.toLowerCase(),' -> 'decode.selector === mandate.selector,' -> 362/0.
(c) 'decoded.spender.toLowerCase() === mandate.beneficiary.toLowerCase(),' -> '... === mandate.principal.toLowerCase(),' -> 362/0.
findings.probe_moved_something: Each edit was verified applied by diff (2 changed lines each) before the run. Liveness of the surrounding region is established by the killed sibling mutations in the same file (EVAL_PURCHASE_BENEFICIARY deletion, EVAL_ALLOWANCE_EFFECT before/after swap, EVAL_ENTITLEMENT_ADVANCED boundary, EVAL_CALL_GRAPH_EXPECTED widening, EVAL_NATIVE_DELTA_MATCHES_VALUE widening — five kills in checks.ts).

findings.title: All four round-five lenses share one scratchpad directory and all four wrote the same baseline.log, clobbering each other's baseline evidence
findings.claim: The scratchpad path in each lens's system prompt is the same directory. Every lens's obvious choice of filename for the mandated baseline run — `scratchpad/baseline.log` — collides. I observed my own baseline log containing the tail of another lens's run (two distinct 'ℹ tests 405' blocks with different duration_ms, and a repeated 'RPC surface' suite), and `pgrep -f scripts/test.sh` showed four concurrent runs from four worktrees all redirecting to that one path. A reviewer who reads baseline.log rather than the exit status of their own process is reading a different worktree's evidence.
findings.why_it_matters: This round's whole method depends on 'RUN THE BASELINE ON AN UNTOUCHED TREE BEFORE YOU RUN ANY PROBE'. If the baseline artifact a lens reads is another lens's, the instrument the round is built on is the one that is unreliable — which is this project's signature defect, reproduced in the review harness rather than in the code. Secondary effect: four concurrent `npm test` runs deadlocked `test/signer.e2e.test.ts` for 10-19 minutes at a stretch (node's `--test-timeout=0` means a hung file never times out), which is why 18 of my 21 survivors are confirmed against 362 of 405 tests rather than all 405.
findings.reproduction: ls -la <scratchpad>/ shows baseline.log, baseline-fast.log, baseline-gate.log, common-brief.md, r5-workflow.js and a secprobe/ directory alongside r5/ — artifacts from at least three other lenses in one directory. `pgrep -fl test.sh` printed four shells, cd-ing into r5/b-claims, r5/a-instrument, r5/c-free and r5/d-evaluator respectively, all with `> <scratchpad>/baseline.log`. `grep -c 'ℹ tests 405' baseline.log` -> 1 while the tail I had read minutes earlier contained two distinct completions. I moved my own work to <scratchpad>/lensD/ and relied on my process's own exit status (EXIT=0) rather than the shared log.
findings.probe_moved_something: n/a — observed directly in the process table and the directory listing, not inferred.

findings.title: The deep-profile corpus stage cannot run in the review worktrees at all, and once made to run, all 50 committed views mismatch on the deployed DemoPay code hash
findings.claim: Two separate obstacles. (1) `const socketPath = join(REPO, ".sentinel", \`corpus-${port}.sock\`)` produces a path longer than macOS's 104-byte sun_path limit from the r5 worktree location, so `npm run corpus` — and therefore `./scripts/test.sh --gate` — aborts with `Error: connect EINVAL .../.sentinel/corpus-9160.sock` before evaluating a single fixture. (2) With the socket repointed to a short path, a clean corpus run in this worktree differs from ALL 50 committed views: `targetCodeHash` / `targetRuntimeCodeHashOnChain` come out 0xc5c3bf29… where the committed views record 0x28b986ea…, and every derived mandateHash moves with it. 0xc5c3bf29… is exactly keccak256 of the `deployedBytecode.object` in the `contracts/out/DemoPay.sol/DemoPay.json` produced by `forge build` here (forge 1.7.1, solc 0.8.28 pinned, via_ir, optimizer 200 — the gate profile changes only fuzz/invariant settings, so the profile is not the cause). contracts/src/demo/DemoPay.sol has not changed since 2026-07-27; the views were regenerated 2026-08-15.
findings.why_it_matters: (1) means no r5 lens can use the deep gate as an oracle, and the round's baseline paragraph does not say so. (2) is either an artifact of this worktree's toolchain or a real staleness — and if it is real, then A-047/A-048's 'committed view FILES verified' stage is RED at HEAD, which would invalidate the corpus provenance claim the gate rests on. I could not distinguish the two: determining it requires building in the live tree at <repo>, which this brief forbids. Reporting it as unresolved rather than guessing.

brief_critique:
Four things, in descending order of how much they cost.

1. THE BASELINE THE BRIEF DECLARES CANNOT ANSWER THE QUESTION THE BRIEF ASKS. The brief fixes the baseline as `./scripts/test.sh` (fast profile) and asks whether mutations "leave the whole suite GREEN". In the fast profile the §7.1 corpus is not executed — the run prints "corpus: not executed. Use --gate; ts/src/corpus/run.ts is covered by nothing else." Since both `evaluate/` module headers and HANDOFF state that the engine's bar is the corpus and explicitly NOT its own suite, "survives a green fast gate" is a strictly weaker claim than it reads, and a reviewer who stopped there would have overclaimed. I had to build the deep-profile arm myself; doing so produced the round's best finding (D-03: the deep arm cannot see verdicts either). A brief that had said "measure against both profiles, and check what the deep corpus stage actually COMPARES" would have pointed straight at it.

2. THE SCOPE EXCLUDES THE THING THAT DECIDES WHETHER A MUTATION IS DETECTABLE. My target was `ts/src/evaluate/**` and `ts/src/decode/**`. Nothing that determines whether a survivor is real lives in either directory — it lives in `scripts/test.sh`'s corpus stage, in `fixtures/corpus/results/`, and in `ts/src/corpus/leakage.ts`'s FORBIDDEN_KEYS. Scoped strictly, this lens would have produced 21 survivors and no explanation for them, which is a list, not a finding. The "a finding outside it is still welcome" sentence is what saved the round; it deserves to be a method note, not a footnote.

3. THE BRIEF NAMES `scripts/mutate.sh` AS COVERING "PARTS OF THIS SURFACE" AND DOES NOT SAY WHICH. Its E-batch already contains a mutation identical to one of my obvious candidates (E11 / policyChecks failures-only). I spent a full 405-test run re-deriving that it is caught. Listing the existing anchors that touch the assigned target — eight D* and eleven E* mutations here — is cheap and would stop each round paying that toll again.

4. THE BRIEF DOES NOT WARN THAT THE FOUR LENSES SHARE ONE SCRATCHPAD. The obvious filename for the mandated baseline run collides across all four (D-11). Since the brief's own most emphatic instruction is to establish a trustworthy baseline before probing, the harness undermines the instruction. Minor and worth fixing: the brief says the target is "roughly 1400 lines"; it is 1534.

coverage_statement:
WHAT I SWEPT. 34 single-file edits applied to the assigned target: 32 behaviour-changing mutations plus 2 harness controls. Distribution across the six target files: ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts 20, ts/src/evaluate/index.ts 4, ts/src/evaluate/jcs.ts 2, ts/src/decode/abi.ts 4, ts/src/evaluate/hashes.ts 0, ts/src/decode/index.ts 0. Every edit was verified applied by diff before the oracle ran, and the harness aborts loudly on a no-op edit or a non-unique anchor (it never fired, but it was armed).

RESULT. 11 of 32 behaviour-changing mutations killed (34%): the mandate half of the action binding, the allowance-effect pre/post-state swap, the entitlement-advanced boundary, the call-graph widening, the native-delta widening, the uintN width, the trailing-bytes acceptance, the JCS ASCII-key widening, the JCS low-surrogate escape, the failureMode constant, and the policyChecks failures-only bundle edit. 21 survived. Of the survivors, 3 (D-01, D-02, D-04) survived the whole 405-test suite; 18 survived 362 of 405; one of the 21 (dropping the zero-hash guard in EVAL_MANDATE_ACTIVE) I judge a probable EQUIVALENT mutant — keccak256 cannot return the zero word — so the honest behaviour-relevant survivor count is 20.

HARNESS VALIDATION, run in both directions before I believed anything. A comment-only edit to ts/src/evaluate/checks.ts SURVIVED at 243/243 (proves the oracle can report survival). Deleting the EVAL_PURCHASE_BENEFICIARY check was KILLED at 242/243 by the test that names it (proves the oracle can report a kill, and that the region is exercised). Eleven further kills, spread across checks.ts, jcs.ts and abi.ts, confirm every file I mutated is under test — so no survivor in this report rests on a file the suite never loads. Both the 243-test and the 362-test oracles were controlled on the untouched tree before the sweep, and the 362 oracle was controlled AGAIN after the last restore (362/362), which is what tells me nothing leaked between runs.

WHAT I LOOKED AT BUT DID NOT MUTATE. ts/src/evaluate/hashes.ts: I read it and reasoned that its import-time golden assertions kill most edits trivially, but I did NOT measure the interesting class there — swapping two SAME-TYPED adjacent fields in hashMandate/hashPolicy (e.g. validAfter/validUntil), which the goldens cannot see and which differential.test.ts probably but not certainly catches. That is an untested hypothesis, not a result. ts/src/decode/index.ts: zero mutations, which is a real hole in my sweep — decodeCall's registry lookup, the selector/target-mismatch branch, decodeBySelector's missing target binding, describe(), and isUnlimitedApproval are unmeasured by me (scripts/mutate.sh's D5-D8 cover parts of that surface, but I did not run them).

WHAT I DID NOT TOUCH AT ALL. Any Solidity; the Python verifier and its 160 tests, 7 samples and 77 tamper cases; the eight workspace guard scripts except reading check-eval-codes.sh and check-class-coverage.sh; the corpus emitter's leakage and rationale guards beyond reading them; the ablation report's published numbers (I noted that D-01 would move "L3 false-allows 1 of 50" to 2 and did not verify it); ts/src/signer/** beyond reading the window and allowlist checks to establish that D-01 and D-02 have a second line of defence; the D-014 signer-side decode attestation; multi-mutation combinations; and any systematic equivalent-mutant analysis beyond the one case I flagged.

WHAT THE NULL SPACE MEANS. This is a bounded sweep, not an exhaustive one, and its shape is my imagination's shape — the same limitation the brief records for implementer-written mutation sets. In particular the 21 survivors are concentrated in exactly the two places I thought to look hardest (conjunction halves and comparison boundaries), which should be read as evidence about where I aimed, not as evidence that the rest of the engine is pinned. Nothing here licenses "the evaluator is sound"; what it licenses is "the engine's happy path and one witness per declared code are pinned, and almost nothing else is."
